With regard to Chamath's points in the previous episode,  mentioned again on this one. I re-post my Twitter reply here (includes a point Alex made)

Chamath's points against Bitcoin: AI could "break SHA-256" and drain Satoshi's wallet, a quantum-resistant migration is "basically impossible" because Bitcoiners can't agree on anything, so it "eventually gets hacked and then it goes to zero." Alex Wissner-Gross added that Anthropic's ECDSA work shows frontier models "can probably achieve astonishing inversion attacks."

Let's take each scenario seriously and see where it leads.

Alex's point first. Anthropic's curve post was not a break, but the trend is real. In July their model improved the best known attacks on HAWK, a post-quantum signature candidate, and on reduced-round AES. AI now does actual cryptanalysis. So assume it one day finds a weakness in secp256k1, the curve behind Bitcoin's signatures. Today the best known attack is still generic, about 2^127 work. If that changed, Bitcoin would need a new signature scheme. It has added one before: Schnorr, with Taproot in 2021, by soft fork.

Now Chamath's SHA-256 scenario. Satoshi's coins don't depend on it. They sit behind public keys, so only a curve break reaches them. A SHA-256 break would most likely show up in mining first: one party finding blocks far faster than everyone else, able to double spend and censor. Serious, but if the shortcut spreads to everyone, difficulty adjusts and mining carries on. If one party keeps it, or it signals a deeper break, the fix is a new hash by hard fork, as Satoshi himself described in 2010. Stealing coins through SHA-256 alone would need a much stronger break.

The scenario we can actually measure is quantum. Google estimates a Bitcoin key could be broken in minutes by fewer than 1,200 error-corrected qubits running about 90 million operations, built from under 500,000 physical qubits. Today's record is 8 error-corrected qubits in a short benchmark, or 48 under a looser definition, and the largest machines running real computations have about 100 to 160 physical qubits. Roadmaps aim higher: IBM and Quantinuum target a few hundred error-corrected qubits by 2029, IBM 2,000 by 2033 or later, and Google wants its own post-quantum migration done by 2029. The gap is large but closing, and roughly 6 to 7M BTC already sit behind exposed public keys.

Bitcoin's first step is drafted. BIP-360 would add a new output type that works like Taproot without the key path, so a coin commits only to a tree of scripts and no public key sits on chain before it is spent. It is a draft with no activation, and it adds no post-quantum signatures yet; those need separate proposals. Users can already help themselves: don't reuse addresses, and keep coins in addresses you have never spent from, which don't reveal a public key (Taproot addresses do).

Notice the pattern. In every case the technical fix is known. What decides the outcome is whether users, developers and miners agree to adopt it in time. That is social consensus, and it is Bitcoin's real security layer, above the cryptography.

So Chamath's coordination worry is the right question. But the record says Bitcoin agrees when it has to. In 2010 a bug created 184 billion BTC and the fix was out within hours. In 2013 a chain split was resolved the same night. Slow and contentious in peacetime, fast in an emergency. That's not a path to zero. Most predictions that Bitcoin goes to zero have not aged well, and I doubt this one will.

“Abundance” describes production, but most human misery comes from distribution, power, and status, and those don’t fix themselves when output goes up.

We already live in abundance by any 1900 standard. The US produces enough food to feed everyone and has more empty housing units than homeless people, yet hunger and homelessness persist. Those are coordination and political problems: zoning, incentives, who owns what, who gets a say. Productivity and wages also tracked together for decades after WWII, then diverged around the 1970s. Technology kept delivering gains; the institutions deciding who captured them changed. Nothing about AI automatically reverses that. If anything, AI may concentrate gains further, because the returns go to whoever owns the models, compute, and data, which is a small number of firms.

On displacement, the strongest version of your point isn’t “jobs vanish forever.” Optimists are right that past waves created new work: agricultural employment went from about 40% to under 2% of the workforce, and we didn’t get 38% permanent unemployment. But “the economy eventually adjusts” hides a lot. The adjustment often happens across generations, not within a worker’s career. The children of displaced farmers got the new jobs. The farmers often didn’t. The research on manufacturing towns hit by trade shocks found lasting drops in earnings, marriage rates, and health, plus rising deaths of despair, in places that never really recovered. A 52-year-old taxi driver doesn’t retrain into prompt engineering, and “the aggregate numbers look fine in 2045” is no comfort to him. The new risk with AI is speed and breadth. Past automation hit specific sectors one at a time, which left somewhere for workers to go. Something that pressures driving, customer service, paralegal work, coding, and design at the same time leaves fewer refuges.

Absolute gains don’t settle things. People care about relative position, security, dignity, and having a role. A world where everyone has a cheap AI doctor but a tiny class owns everything productive, and most people have no economic leverage, is materially comfortable and politically fragile. Labor’s bargaining power has historically been what forced elites to share: unions, the threat of strikes, the need for mass armies and workforces. If human labor stops being necessary, that lever weakens, and distribution depends on the goodwill of owners or the strength of democratic institutions. That’s a precarious basis for utopia.

The Core Cycle of Science

Let's get real about the difficulties facing putting data centers in outer space, and even on the Moon, as a viable alternative to placing them on Earth. Consider this:

What are the physics in terms of economic practicality, for cooling data centers in  outerspace?

The concept of orbital data centers is often promoted on the premise that "space is cold," but this misunderstands fundamental thermodynamics. In terms of economic practicality, the physics of cooling in space represents a massive economic bottleneck due to the absence of matter for convective heat transfer, forcing absolute reliance on highly inefficient radiative cooling.
The transition from terrestrial fluid dynamics to orbital thermodynamics drastically spikes the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) for space-based computing.

1. The Governing Physics: Convective vs. Radiative Cooling

On Earth, data centers dump waste heat into the atmosphere or water sources via conduction and convection. Air or water molecules directly touch hot heat sinks, carry the heat away, and use the Earth as an effectively infinite cold reservoir.
In the vacuum of space, there is no air or water. Convection is impossible. The only way to reject heat is through thermal radiation. This process is governed by the Stefan-Boltzmann Law:
\(\.{Q}_{\text{rad}}=\varepsilon \sigma AT^{4}\)
Where:
• \(\.{Q}_{\text{rad}}\) is the heat rejection rate (Watts)
• ε is the surface emissivity (0 to 1)
• σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant (5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²K⁴)
• A is the radiator surface area (m²)
• T is the absolute temperature in Kelvin
Because heat leaves solely as weak infrared radiation, the rate of heat rejection is brutally slow compared to Earth.

2. The Scaling Problem (The T⁴ Penalty)

Silicon chips generally must be kept below 80°C (353 K) to operate safely and prevent permanent damage.
• At a standard operating temperature of 20°C (293 K), a two-sided radiator panel emits only about 633 Watts per square meter.
• For context, a single modern AI server rack can draw 40 to 100 kW of power, and a single NVIDIA H100 GPU requires roughly 1.1 m² of dedicated radiator area just to survive.
When scaled to industrial levels, the geometric requirements explode:

Data Center Scale	Required Radiator Surface Area	Terrestrial Equivalent
1 Megawatt (Puny/Edge)	≈ 1,200 to 1,600 m²	A standard hockey rink
100 Megawatts (Medium)	≈ 200,000 m²	30 to 40 football fields
1 Gigawatt (Hyperscale AI)	≈ 2,000,000 m²	A small city center

Furthermore, these calculations assume a "perfect" environment. In Low Earth Orbit (LEO), radiators are constantly bombarded by external thermal fluxes—direct solar radiation, solar reflection off the Earth (albedo), and the Earth's own infrared heat emission (≈ 400 W/m²). To keep the radiators from absorbing more heat than they emit, complex multi-layer insulation and active, motorized sun-tracking geometry are required, adding immense dead-weight.

3. Economic Implications of the Physics

The constraints of the Stefan-Boltzmann law dictate the commercial viability of these systems.
• Astronomical Launch Costs: Space-grade radiator panels weigh approximately 5 to 9 kg/m². To cool a modest 40 MW facility, the radiator mass alone would require dozens of dedicated heavy-lift rocket launches, costing billions of dollars just for the cargo transit before accounting for the cost of the hardware itself.
• Active Fluid Maintenance Overhead: Terrestrial data centers use simple plumbing. Moving heat from dense chips to sprawling space radiators requires closed-loop liquid pumping systems. In microgravity, fluid dynamics suffer from bubble formation, seal degradation from extreme thermal cycles, and micro-meteoroid puncture risks. Because on-orbit maintenance is currently impossible, companies must launch massive amounts of redundant cooling loops, compounding the initial launch costs.
• The Solar-Radiator Catch-22: Generating power in space requires massive solar arrays. However, the larger the solar array, the more solar radiation it catches, and the more structural mass is introduced. This creates a geometric explosion: a massive array creates a giant thermal footprint, requiring an even larger radiator array, which in turn increases the drag and structural load of the satellite.
